profiles.meeting_scenario: At a European multiline insurer, a small brainstorming meeting is being held between Group Capital Management and Business Performance to generate candidate ways to test a recovery-based solvency lens inspired by recent academic work on Recovery Value at Risk before the next ORSA planning cycle. The context is that the CFO has asked for ideas that could both strengthen the firm's creditor-protection narrative with regulators and potentially improve how capital is allocated to business divisions. The agenda is to sketch what a 'pilot' could look like, what existing benchmarks it should be compared against, which liabilities or claimholders it should cover, and whether the firm can build it quickly from existing analytics. The expected outcome is not a final design, but a short list of promising pilot concepts and a rough plan for who will socialize the idea with the CFO and Chief Risk Officer.

members.name: Elena Rossi
members.expertise: Solvency II, ORSA design, legal-entity capital frameworks, board-level capital communication
members.background: Elena spent eight years in regulatory policy advisory before joining the insurer's group finance function, where she now translates emerging solvency concepts into proposals that can be discussed with the CFO, CRO, and supervisors.
members.private_state: She wants a low-friction concept note that the CFO can endorse quickly, without reopening the firm's formal capital model or creating expectations of a large systems project this year.
hidden_assumptions: A 'pilot' for a new solvency idea is usually a narrow desktop exercise using the latest year-end legal-entity balance sheet and existing ORSA outputs, not a live management tool.
When people say 'current benchmark' or 'historic standard' in this context, they mean the Solvency II-style policyholder protection benchmark already used in external regulatory conversations.
A recovery-based creditor metric for an insurer should mainly be framed around policyholder claims at the regulated operating entity, because that is what supervisors care about first.
If the team says they can 'use existing stress outputs,' they will naturally rely on annual ORSA scenario files and exclude discretionary future management actions unless those are already locked in.

members.name: Marcus Lee
members.expertise: Capital allocation, divisional performance steering, planning models, insurance cash-flow analytics
members.background: Marcus came from a consulting and actuarial analytics background and now runs the models used for quarterly business planning, return-on-capital comparisons, and business-unit scorecards across the group.
members.private_state: He wants to turn the idea into something the business heads will find operationally useful, ideally a shadow metric that can influence next quarter's planning discussions and strengthen his team's role in capital steering.
hidden_assumptions: A 'pilot' is only worth attention if at least one or two business units can see their own numbers in it during the planning cycle.

When senior people ask for calibration to the 'current benchmark,' they usually want consistency with the firm's internal economic capital and rating-agency narrative, not just statutory solvency language.

If a recovery metric is meant to influence divisional incentives, the relevant claims base should include all economically exposed creditors in the capital chain, including holdco funding and material intragroup claims.

If the team says they can 'use existing stress outputs,' the obvious source is the quarterly planning and earnings-at-risk infrastructure, including assumed management actions and business-unit cash-flow projections.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They repeatedly agree to start with a 'pilot.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena means a limited concept demonstration for senior management: one legal entity, year-end data, a few comparison charts against existing solvency metrics, and no operational embedding.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus means a practical shadow implementation: at least two business units, quarterly planning data, and outputs that managers could react to in the next planning round.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In strategy meetings, 'pilot' is a socially safe word that signals prudence and experimentation, so neither person feels a need to unpack scale, audience, or operational depth unless the project is already approved.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the new measure should be compared with or calibrated to the firm's 'current benchmark' and 'historic standard.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena is thinking of the firm's external regulatory anchor: the Solvency II 99.5% one-year framework and the policyholder-protection standard referenced in prior regulator-facing materials.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus is thinking of the firm's internal capital benchmark used in planning and rating discussions: the tighter economic-capital hurdle the CFO cited in last year's divisional capital review.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both benchmarks are long-standing, widely used, and often discussed in the same meetings, so the phrases 'current benchmark' and 'historic standard' feel fully shared even though each person silently defaults to a different one.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the exercise should focus on 'recovery on creditors' claims' and improve the firm's 'creditor-protection story.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena assumes the scope is the regulated insurer's external policyholder and senior creditor claims at the legal-entity level, because that is the conventional solvency-regulation perimeter.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus assumes the scope includes economically relevant claims across the group funding chain, including holdco debt and significant intragroup obligations, because otherwise the metric will not work for divisional capital steering.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'creditors' claims' sounds precise enough on the surface, and both scopes are defensible in the broader corporate context, so the conversation can proceed smoothly without either person noticing the perimeter mismatch.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the idea should be built quickly by 'using existing stress outputs' rather than creating a new model stack.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena assumes the team will repurpose the annual ORSA stress package and legal-entity balance sheet outputs, with limited rework and without layering in fresh management-action assumptions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus assumes the team will pull from the quarterly planning engine and cash-flow stress files, including management actions already embedded in divisional forecasts.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both teams really do have 'existing stress outputs,' and reusing current infrastructure sounds like obvious good practice, so neither side thinks to specify which library, timing basis, or action set is being taken as the default.

turns.inner_thought: The CFO is asking for something he can nod through quickly before the ORSA cycle starts in earnest. I need to frame this as a modest pilot, really a concept demonstration, not anything that sounds like a redesign of the capital framework or a live steering tool. And the creditor-protection angle should stay close to the regulated entity story, because that is what lands cleanly with supervisors.
